fix: keep a completed download's outcome until the activity ends

Two faults CodeRabbit found in the scan-to-scan bookkeeping.

A download that finished while another was still writing had its
outcome thrown away. The scan that sees its temporary file go still has
active work, so it returns early and `disappearedFiles` is rebuilt from
the next scan onwards -- and if the last remaining download was then
cancelled, nothing was left to have completed and the activity closed
outright with no completion shown. Vanished files are now held until
nothing is being written, and judged together at that point.

Separately, a partial file present at launch is ignored by name so a
download already running when the app starts does not claim an activity
of its own -- but the name was never released. A later download that
happened to reuse it was ignored for the life of the process. The name
is freed when the original file goes.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix: give the collapsed volume row the height it actually needs

Trimming the volume row's reserve to 32 pinned the capsule against the
panel's bottom edge with lyrics off. The arithmetic was done on the row
alone -- a 13pt capsule under a 14pt gap -- but the panel's fixed
content already runs over the height it is given: a 60pt header, a 13pt
progress row and a 58pt transport row, with the stack's gaps and insets,
come to 188 against 152pt of content height. The volume row has to carry
that 12pt too, so 40.

The dead space that started this was in the lyrics reserve, not this
one: 64pt held for a row that draws 8pt of inset, two 15pt lines and the
same 14pt gap. That is 56 now.

fix: show the battery percentage inside the icon outside minimalistic mode

The setting was disabled unless Minimalistic UI was on, and would not
have done anything if it were reachable: `BatteryView` has taken a
`showPercentInside` all along and draws the number inside the body, but
only the minimalist pill ever passed one. The standard notch's battery
now passes it too.

The toggle is gated on the notch showing a battery at all rather than on
which of the two styles is drawn, and the separate percentage beside the
icon stands down when the number is inside it, so it is not shown twice.

fix: let the completion animation finish

`isDownloading` stays true for the two seconds the completion animation
runs, so a scan during that window found no active files and nothing
left in the vanished set, concluded the download had been cancelled, and
closed the view mid-animation. A directory event in that window is
likely rather than hypothetical -- the rename that finishes a download
is itself one.

The old completion test happened to be safe here: its close branch was
only reached when a file had disappeared *and* none had appeared, which
a follow-up scan does not satisfy. Rewriting it around the vanished set
lost that, so the animation is now guarded explicitly.

fix: require the destination to have been written, not merely present

A download told to replace a file already on disk starts with a
destination full of the old file's bytes. Cancelling it then looked
exactly like finishing: something non-empty was sitting at the target
name. Completion now compares the destination's modification date
against what it was when the temporary file appeared, so only a
destination this download actually wrote counts.

The stamp is captured when a temporary file first shows up and only
then; taking it later would record what the download had already put
there. A missing entry means there was nothing at that name, or nothing
with anything in it, which is still a completion.

fix: stop the artwork clip cutting the corner off the source badge

The badge is meant to overhang the artwork's bottom-right, but a
clipShape wrapped around the whole stack trimmed it flush. That clip was

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix: stop the position counting paused time as played

Measured against the running adapter: Spotify anchors once when a track
starts and then publishes nothing for the rest of it. A capture 141
seconds into a track reported an elapsed time of 0 with a timestamp 141
seconds old -- the anchor from when it began.

Extrapolating from that is right while the music runs, because
wall-clock and playback time advance together. They stop agreeing the
moment playback stops. A pause the sender does not follow with a fresh
position leaves the anchor where it was, so resuming counts the paused
time as played, and every pause pushes the estimate further ahead --
which is why the only way to bring it back was to pause and play until
the sender happened to republish.

The position is re-anchored on the transition itself: frozen where it
had got to when playback stops, restarted from there when it resumes.

fix: draw the LIVE indicator the way Apple draws it

Apple runs the line through the word: two thin rules meeting a plain
LIVE in the middle, softening as they run away from it. This drew a 10pt
capsule with a fill, a centre shade, a stroke and three blend modes,
then dropped shadowed text over the whole thing -- which reads as a
progress bar someone has written on, and a stream has no progress to
draw. The bar was also sized like a track you could scrub, which is the
one thing it is not.

One component behind the notch, the lock screen player and the floating
window, so all three follow.

fix: require a newer destination, and close the view when switched off

Completion accepted any change to the destination's modification date.
Later is the test, not different: a destination that comes out older
than it was when the download started was not written by that download,
something restored or copied an earlier file over the name.

And switching the listener off during a download left the live activity
on screen. `stopMonitoring` clears `isDownloading`, which is the flag
`updateDownloadingState` checks before doing anything, so the call after
it was a no-op and nothing ever told the coordinator to close.

fix: do not format a duration a track could not have

The remaining-time label subtracts the position from whatever duration
arrived and formats the result as hours, so a sender handing back an
epoch timestamp instead of a length -- which is one of the things they
do when there is no length to give, as on a live stream -- came out on
screen as -1732919508:00:54.

A duration outside a day is treated as unreported, and both labels show
--:-- instead. The formatter also stops converting a non-finite or
out-of-range value to Int, which traps rather than printing nonsense.

fix: draw the charge fill proportionally

The fill was floored at the body's height, on the reasoning that it

fix: guard the slider's range, not just the labels

Guarding the formatting left the range alone, and `0 ... duration` traps
when the upper bound is below the lower one -- verified: `0.0 ... -5.0`
crashes on construction. So a negative duration took the app down before

fix: send the lyrics list back to the top when a new track starts

Whether it rewound was a coincidence. A new track resets the current line
to -1, and the scroll was guarded on that index having a row of its own --
which only tracks opening with an intro long enough to earn a note marker
ever have. Every other song left the list parked wherever the last one had
scrolled it to.

The handler that rebuilds the rows for a new track never scrolled at all:
it was attached outside the ScrollViewReader, so it had no proxy. Both it
and the duration handler move inside.

A missing row now means staying put only mid-track, where the words on
screen are still the right ones. Before the first line it means going to
the first row there is.

fix: stop replaying the pause into the playback position

The re-anchor added for this only ran when the sender published no
position at all. Spotify publishes one -- it just never publishes a fresh
one. Four reads six seconds apart on a paused track returned the same
elapsed of 40.342 paired with a timestamp 235, 241, 247 and 254 seconds
old, still climbing: it is republishing the instant it paused.

That pair is true, and harmless while paused, because nothing extrapolates
a stopped track. It goes wrong the moment playback resumes, with the
anchor still pointing to before the pause and the whole stopped interval
counted as played.

The question was never whether the sender sent a position. It is whether
it sent a current one, which is now decided by how old the timestamp
beside it is. On a play-state change without a current sample the anchor
is re-stamped at the transition -- and the transition instant is now,
unless the sender's own timestamp is about now too.

fix: close two races in the lock screen HUD handover, and document the gaps

isLockedSnapshot was nonisolated(unsafe) with a main-actor writer, by way
of isLocked's didSet, and readers on whatever threads CoreAudio and the
brightness watcher happen to use. That is a data race that only looked
benign because a Bool is one word wide. It is behind an
OSAllocatedUnfairLock now, matching SystemOSDManager.

The record of which lock state the native HUD had been handed over for was
kept by the caller and written before the call. The callee can decline --
it guards on setup being complete and an observer existing -- so a request
dropped that way still counted as applied, and every later request for the
same state returned early on the strength of it. A lock that arrived
before setup finished therefore left the HUD in the wrong hands for the
rest of the session. The comparison now lives with the code that applies
it, behind the readiness guard, and is cleared when the observer restarts,
since a fresh observer carries none of the old one's suppression.

fix: give the keyboard backlight toggles back when the provider quits

resolvedControlFlags() hands the keys to the external display app only
while integration is enabled and the provider is actually running, so
quitting the provider returns them to Atoll. The four keyboard backlight
gates were reading the integration setting alone, which left them greyed
out over settings that had started working again -- the same mistake this
branch already fixed for the volume and brightness steppers.

They share one modifier now rather than a copy of the ownership test each.
It carries the observation of both providers with it, so the controls
re-enable the moment the provider quits, which a plain computed property
in three different views would not have done without each of them
observing the managers itself.

docs: state the whole usable-duration rule in the changelog

"Outside a day" reads as an upper bound alone, which leaves out the zero,
negative and non-finite durations the guard also rejects and the crash it
was written for.

refactor: one threshold for what counts as an instrumental break

The list decided which rows to draw as a break and MusicManager decided
whether playback was in one, each from its own copy of the same five
seconds. Nothing disagreed while both said 5, which is exactly how long
that lasts. The list reads the manager's constant now.

docs: document what the popover activity reporters do

The four of them carried implementation notes but no docstring, so the
thing worth knowing from outside -- that each reports its own popover
under its own token, because the notch must stay open while any picker is
showing -- was only discoverable by reading the view model.

docs: say what the 10-of-10 comparison was against

"Against 10 of 10 without it" leaves the reader to infer that the second
figure counts the opposite outcome. Say that the panel appeared in all ten.

docs: name the thing the glyphs were sized by

"The same number" is vague where the very next sentence is about point
size against optical size. Say point size.

feat: notice Opera downloads as well

Opera is Chromium underneath but names its half-finished files
.opdownload rather than .crdownload, so the watcher never saw one and
nothing downloaded in Opera raised a live activity. Nothing else needed
changing: the destination is still the name with the extension taken off,
and the completion test never cared which browser wrote the file.

fix: one swipe, one skip

A trackpad delivers a flick as a run of touch events followed by a run of
momentum ones, and the gesture was ended between the two. The momentum
tail then accumulated from zero against the same threshold the touch had
just crossed, so the action fired again -- one swipe skipping two tracks.

Momentum is the end of a flick the user has already let go of, not new
input, so it no longer counts toward the threshold. The open and close
gestures were double-firing the same way.

The cost is that a very light flick which only reached the threshold once
momentum carried it now needs a slightly longer swipe.

fix: don't put a stranger's lyrics on an untagged track

An untagged rip reports itself as "Track 7" by "Unknown artist". lrclib
holds twenty other untagged rips filed under exactly that title and
artist, so the search came back with an exact match on both fields --
and one of them, Beyonce's "If I Were a Boy", scrolled past during
somebody else's song.

Scoring cannot fix this, because the scores are perfect. The question
has to be asked before the search: this metadata names a position on a
disc, not a song, so there is nothing to look up. LyricsLookupKey now
refuses it the same way it already refuses empty fields.

The floor in bestLyricsMatch is the smaller, separate half. Search
ranks, it does not filter, so lrclib returns its closest guess even when
that guess shares nothing with the track playing. Requiring the winner
to agree on both the title and the artist keeps covers and unrelated
songs out; agreeing on the title alone is how karaoke versions get in.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix: filter lyrics results before ranking, and fold both sides

Two problems with the floor added in the previous commit, both found in
review.

Ranking first and checking the winner afterwards throws away a good row
whenever a bad one outscores it. A wrong artist with an exactly matching
title, album and synced lyrics scores higher than the right artist
matched only by containment -- the wrong row won, failed the check, and
the correct lyrics were never considered. Filter to candidates, then
rank what is left.

The second is older than this PR. The request is diacritic-folded before
it is sent, so lrclib is searched for "Beyonce", but the response comes
back spelled "Beyoncé". Only one side was folded, which quietly cost a
scoring bonus for years and, once agreement became mandatory, rejected
the correct lyrics outright. Both sides now go through the same
normalization.

The matching moved to LyricsSearchResults so it can be tested without a
MusicManager: six cases covering accented fields in both directions, the
high-scoring wrong artist, and the floor itself.

fix: require text on both sides before scoring the album

Containment against an empty needle is decided by which overload
resolves, not by intent. It happens to be false today with Foundation
imported, so nothing was mis-scored, but the album is the one field
nothing filters on -- the title and artist are already non-empty by the

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix: don't accept a re-recording in place of the track playing

Containment is deliberately loose, so "Crimewave (Sped Up)" agrees with
a request for "Crimewave". Usually that costs nothing -- an exact title
outscores a suffixed one, so the plain row wins whenever it exists --
but when the variant is all lrclib holds, the words are right and every
timing is wrong, which is the drift this PR set out to stop.

Rejecting only markers the request does not itself carry keeps the
reverse case working: playing the sped-up version still finds the
sped-up lyrics.

Exact title equality would have been the simpler rule and is wrong here.
The request has "(remastered)", "(live)", "(mono)" and "(feat. ...)"
stripped before it is sent, so a row carrying those suffixes is exactly
what the stripping went looking for -- requiring equality would reject
it. Those four are deliberately absent from the marker list, and a test
pins that.

Markers match on word boundaries, so "Undercover Martyn" is not a cover.

fix: refuse re-recordings as well as remixes

A re-recording is the case the marker list missed. "Crimewave
(Re-Recorded)" and "(Taylor's Version)" are the same words performed
again, at timings that are not the requested track's.

"'s version" is matched rather than a bare "version" on purpose: the
possessive is what distinguishes an artist re-recording their catalogue
from "(Album Version)", which is simply the track. A test pins that
album and single versions still match.

Markers deliberately anchor only their leading word boundary, so each
one covers its own inflections -- "remix" already caught "remixed", and
"re-record" now catches "re-recorded" and "re-recording" -- while the
leading boundary keeps "undercover" from being a cover. The comment said
this; it now says why.

perf: ask the kernel for OSDUIHelper instead of forking pgrep

The OSD suppression watcher runs for the entire life of the app and asks
once a second whether OSDUIHelper is up. It asked by spawning
/usr/bin/pgrep: a fork, an exec, a pipe and a process reap to answer a
question the kernel answers directly.

Measured, 60 calls each: pgrep 66.6ms per call, proc_listpids 0.60ms --
about 110x. In CPU terms the old path cost ~5ms per call once a second,
so roughly half a percent of a core, continuously, forever. Sampling an
idle app for 15 seconds put osduiHelperPID at 482 samples, the largest
single consumer in the process; after the change the same sample shows
21.

pgrep -n means newest by start time rather than highest PID. The two
agree until PIDs wrap, so the replacement reads the start time from
PROC_PIDTBSDINFO and compares that rather than assuming the ordering.
Both forms were checked against the same live helper and returned the
same PID.

isOSDUIHelperRunning was a third spawn asking the same question and now
shares the one implementation.

perf: only republish the playback anchor when it moves

timestampDate was the one unguarded assignment in
updateFromPlaybackState -- every neighbour compares before assigning,
this one did not. It is @Published and read by the notch, the
minimalist player and the lock screen panel, so each delivery from the
media stream invalidated all of them.

The name invites the assumption that it always changes. It does not: it
is the playback anchor, moving when the player re-anchors, which Spotify
does about once a track. While paused it re-sends the same instant
indefinitely -- four samples taken six seconds apart during this work
carried a byte-identical timestamp. Nearly every assignment was writing
a value that had not moved.

Assigning the same Date was already a no-op for
estimatedPlaybackPosition, which is the only reader that computes from
it, so the guard changes nothing except how often observers hear about
it.

fix: a volume that cannot be read is not a volume of zero

getVolume() initialised its result to 0 and returned it whether or not
the read succeeded, in both the no-element branch and the final
fallback. Zero is a real volume, so an unreadable device was
indistinguishable from a silent one: the slider dropped to the bottom
and stayed there, and the glyph showed muted.

Two changes. The level is now also read through
kAudioHardwareServiceDeviceProperty_VirtualMainVolume ('vmvc') -- the
property macOS's own volume UI works through, which outputs that publish
no per-channel VolumeScalar still answer. And when every read fails the
last known level is held instead of a fabricated zero, so a failed read
does nothing rather than lying.

setVolume takes the same fallback, since a scalar nobody accepted does
not mean the volume cannot be set.

Reported by StudioKeys against the lock screen player on internal
speakers. Not reproducible on this Mac -- its speakers answer
VolumeScalar on the main element (0.3125, matching the system's 31%) --
which is consistent with it depending on how a particular output
publishes its volume. Verified here only that the reading is unchanged
where it already worked.

Follow-up to #750.

fix: stop the lock screen volume capsule sitting on the panel border

The collapsed panel reserved 220pt. Measured, its content stack is
192.5pt, which with the 16pt and 12pt insets needs 220.5 -- so the last
half point was clipped and the capsule sat on the bottom border, while
the transport row above it kept roughly 33pt of air. Four times the gap
above as below is what "the volume bar sticks to the bottom" looks like.

The old constant was derived from an assumed 12pt overrun of the 180pt
base; the real figure is 13.5. Rather than re-derive it I measured the
laid-out stack and sized from that, and left enough over that the
capsule has about 20pt beneath it instead of nothing.

fix: observe the virtual volume too, and remember levels per device

Two gaps in the fallback added a commit ago, both found in review.

The fallback exists for devices with no scalar volume element -- which
are exactly the devices that had nothing to install a listener on. They
would read correctly once and then never hear about a change made
anywhere else: the keyboard keys, Control Centre, another app. The
virtual main volume is now observed as well when the device publishes
it.

The remembered level was a single value shared by every device.
Headphones at 20% and speakers at 80% are two different facts, so
answering one with the other after a route change is a fresh way of
being wrong. It is keyed by device now, with the most recent reading of
any device kept as the last resort for one that has never answered --
"unchanged" beats "silent" when the truth is "unknown".

Installing the listeners also now takes down the previous ones first.
That was already wrong before this PR -- route changes stacked another
live pair on a device no longer being read, each still calling
notifyCurrentState -- and adding a third listener would have made it
worse.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix: refuse a relative volume change with nothing to be relative to

getVolume answers with another device's level rather than report a zero
it does not mean. That is the right call for showing a slider and the
wrong one for adjust(by:), which adds a delta to it and writes the
result: being sixty points out about the base moves the volume sixty
points.

So the guess stays where it is useful and is refused where it is
dangerous. adjust(by:) now requires a confirmed reading for the device
it is adjusting -- it reads on the way through, so any device able to
answer populates its own entry first, and only one that has never
answered is turned away. Absolute sets from the slider are untouched;
just the delta is refused.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix: read one device per volume read, not one per lookup

currentDeviceID is written on callbackQueue when the route changes and
read wherever a volume is asked for, which is any thread. getVolume took
a snapshot for the cache key but each helper below it went back to the
property, so a route change part-way through a read could take the level
from device B and file it under device A -- the precise mix-up the
per-device memory was added to avoid.

The read path now carries one device through: getVolume snapshots once
and passes it to readScalarVolume, readVirtualMainVolume, volumeElements
and the getData helpers, which take it as an override rather than
consulting the property themselves.

The property itself is behind a lock as well, so the readers that still
consult it are not racing the writer for the bytes.

fix: let the lyrics lead the voice by a quarter second

A line that arrives exactly on its timestamp arrives too late to read:
the word is already being sung by the time the eye finds it.

This used to happen by accident. A stale playback anchor made the
position estimate run ahead of the music, so lines flipped early and the
lyrics felt well timed even while the clock beside them was wrong.
Fixing the anchor made every line land exactly on its timestamp, which
reads as late -- an improvement in accuracy that was a regression in
feel.

So the lead is kept and made deliberate: a quarter second, applied once
to the position every lyric decision is taken from, so the index, the
sweep and the instrumental-break test all move together.

fix: write the volume to one device, and remember what was written

The read path already took a single device snapshot; the write path did
not. Element discovery, the scalar write and the virtual-main fallback
each looked the current device up for themselves, so a route change
between those steps aimed one device's elements at another. setVolume
now takes the device as a parameter, and adjust(by:) passes the device
it read its base level from.

A successful write also records the level it wrote. notifyCurrentState
reads straight afterwards, and when that read fails getVolume answered
with the level from before the write -- so the slider sprang back to
where it had just been dragged from.

Mute moves with it: setMuted and getMuteState take the same device, since
setVolume consults and changes mute as part of the same write.

fix: do not report a volume of zero before one has ever been read

The per-device memory held the last known level so a failed read said
nothing new rather than claiming silence, but the memory it fell back to
started at zero -- so the one moment with no last known level, the first
read at launch, was exactly the moment that published 0%. An output that
cannot answer at startup showed the slider at the bottom, which is a
real volume and reads as the user having turned it down.

The last-resort level is now absent until some device has answered, and
the state notification says nothing at all while it is. Callers that
must produce a number still fall back to zero; callers that are telling
somebody else what the volume is no longer do.

fix: keep pinned images, purge unpinned ones, and keep the tests off the real store

Four things from review, all of them real.

Pinning an image while history was not being saved wrote a pinned record
naming a file that had never existed: the bytes were in memory only, so
a restart restored a pinned entry with no picture in it. Pinning is a
request to keep one thing, so that one image now gets a file. The rest
of the session-only history stays in memory, since none of it was asked
to be kept.

The launch purge took the stored list and left the pictures. Those are
separate files, and the purge runs at launch precisely because the
manager is lazy -- so nothing else deleted them either, and images a
user had asked not to keep sat in Documents for the whole session. Files
a saved pinned item refers to are kept, read from disk because there is
no manager yet to ask.

Two searchable settings pointed at controls that are not always drawn.
"Save History Across Restarts" now takes you to "Enable Clipboard
Manager" and "Widget layout" to "Show lock screen weather", so a search
result lands on something visible rather than nothing.

Worst of the four: the transition tests turned persistence off against
the real store, which deletes every unpinned image file in the clipboard
data directory -- so running the suite deleted the clipboard images of
whoever ran it, and left the stored lists as the last test wrote them.
The data directory is now redirectable and the tests point it at a
temporary one; the stored history and pinned lists are snapshotted and
put back.

fix: dismiss the custom OSD when it is switched off

Switching HUD variants sets enableCustomOSD to false, but nothing was
watching it. A window that happened to be on screen at that moment had
only its own two-second auto-hide left to dismiss it, and switching
outran that -- so the overlay stayed on screen until the app was
restarted. tearDown() existed for this and had no callers.

The manager now observes the setting and dismisses every visible window
the moment the OSD is turned off, and does the same per control when
volume, brightness or keyboard backlight OSDs are switched off
individually. initialize() became idempotent so the observers register
once.

a new OSD re-showed while the fade was still running, which could blank
an OSD that had just appeared.

feat: show the day's temperature range on the lock screen gauge

fix: make the settings panel navigable again

Four things, all in the settings panel.

The Controls tab was the odd one out: its root was a bare VStack where
every other tab roots in a Form, and the variant switch inside it opened
further nested Forms. That gave it a title that stayed highlighted
unlike every other tab, and two independent scroll areas inside one
pane. Rooting it in a Form and turning the nested Forms into Groups
fixes that -- and introduces a second problem in the process. The four
HUD variant cards are a fixed 110pt each, and a fixed width inside a
grouped Form becomes a hard minimum width for the whole pane, so
roughly 490pt of cards forced the settings panel wider than it is and
shoved everything sideways. The cards were always that wide; it only
became a layout constraint once the tab became a Form. They fit to the
available width now and scroll when there is not enough. Both halves
are here together because the second only exists because of the first.

The Lock Screen tab held fourteen sections, ten of which configure one
widget each, so the global settings were buried among the per-widget
ones. It is split into General and Widgets. Settings search still opens
any setting directly: the section each one lives on is recorded in the
search index itself, which is the table you already have to edit to make
a setting searchable, so a setting cannot be listed for search and
mis-routed at the same time. That index moved to file scope to make it
readable from the tab.

The segmented pickers are the app's own control rather than the stock
one -- a rounded selection that slides between options on a spring
instead of a flat rectangle that snaps, matching the clipboard panel's
tabs. It keeps the accent colour, so it still follows System Settings.

under it, the music source block gained the same scroll hint the other
scrollable blocks have, the lock screen positioning footer and reminder

feat: favorite the playing song on Apple Music, not just Spotify

The heart control existed but only ever worked for Spotify, because
Spotify was the only source that could favourite. The blocker on Apple
Music was thought to be an Apple Music subscription; it is not one.
Music.app is scriptable and favouriting is a plain read/write property
on its current track -- no MusicKit, no developer token, no
subscription. Atoll already drives Music.app by AppleScript for
playback, so this is the same road.

Favouriting is now a capability on MediaControllerProtocol rather than
a brand: controllers that can do it say so, MusicManager asks whichever
source is playing, and the rest inherit defaults that decline. The old
code named Spotify inline in MusicManager, which is why adding a second
source meant rewriting it rather than extending it.

The Now Playing source needed care. It fronts whatever app is playing
rather than one the user picked, so it dispatches on the playing app's
bundle identifier: Music.app takes the AppleScript path, Spotify the
Web API path. That is also how Spotify favouriting already behaved --
the old code keyed off the playing app -- so putting the logic on the
Spotify controller alone would have quietly broken it for anyone using
Now Playing, which is most people.

Capability is two questions, not one. canEverFavorite decides whether
the control is offered in settings and kept in the slot layout, and
must hold still: nobody should find the option missing from the palette
because the music is stopped or because they have not connected their
account yet. supportsFavoriting decides only whether it is enabled
right now. Conflating them meant the control vanished from settings
exactly when a user went looking for it.

TIDAL, YouTube Music, Amazon Music and Now Playing on any other app
have no favouriting we can reach without shipping OAuth per service, so
they decline and the control is filtered out rather than shown dead.

The label reads Favorite Song rather than Like Song, since one control
now serves both services and Like is Spotify's word for it.

Closes #599

feat: favorite the playing song on YouTube Music

The desktop app's API server plugin exposes the like button directly:
GET /api/v1/like-state reports LIKE, DISLIKE or INDIFFERENT, and
POST /api/v1/like presses the button. There is no account to connect
and no track id to resolve -- the endpoints act on whatever is playing,
and Atoll is already authenticated with the app for playback control.

Because the endpoint presses rather than sets, writing a state reads the
current one first and only presses when the two differ; a state that
cannot be read fails rather than guessing, so the optimistic toggle in
MusicManager rolls back instead of landing on the opposite of the ask.

Also carries the song's videoId into the playback state, giving the
source a stable track identity for lookup staleness instead of the
title/artist/album fallback.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

feat: favorite the playing song on TIDAL

TIDAL offers none of the doors the other sources do. Asked directly,
it registers seven MediaRemote commands and not one of them is a like
or a rating; it is an Electron app with no scripting dictionary; and it
opens no local port. What it does have is an accessibility tree, and the
now playing heart sits in it as a real control -- an AXCheckBox under
#footerPlayer that answers AXPress.

Reading the state is the awkward half. AXValue is empty and AXSelected
stays 0 in both states, and the icon keeps its class either way, because
TIDAL swaps the shape inside the SVG rather than the element. The label
is the only thing that moves, so that is what we read; outside the
languages we recognise the state is reported as unknown rather than
guessed, which leaves the heart dimmed but still pressable.

The control is a toggle, so the press is made only when the current
state differs from the request, and the label is re-read afterwards
because it follows the network round trip rather than the press.

The favouriting members move onto FilteredNowPlayingController so
TidalController can override them: the conformance lives on the base
class, so a witness taken from the protocol extension would win over
anything a subclass declared.

feat: favourite the current song in Cider

Cider already worked as a media source, but only for playback: it is
followed through macOS Now Playing, which carries no favourite command,
so the Favorite Song control had nothing to call and stayed inert.

Cider exposes a local HTTP API for external applications, and it answers
both halves of the question -- `now-playing` reports `inFavorites`, and
`set-rating` writes one back. So unlike TIDAL, where the heart has to be
a read-only indicator because the app accepts no write, Cider's heart is
live.

Un-favouriting sends rating 0 rather than -1. A dislike is a separate
opinion in Apple Music and would follow the user around their
recommendations, which is not what clearing a favourite should mean.

The token goes in an `apptoken` header, bare. Cider's own documentation
names that header `apitoken`, which its server does not accept -- there
is a test pinning this, since it is the detail most likely to regress.

Every failure -- Cider closed, its API switched off, a rejected token,
nothing playing -- reads as unknown rather than as "not favourited", so
the heart never shows a confident wrong answer. `canEverFavorite` stays
true regardless, so the control keeps its place in the palette while
Cider is closed.

fix: do not report a download rate across a completed download

Two lifecycle holes in the speed sampler, both found in review.

The rate was rejected only when the aggregate byte count fell. A
download ending takes its bytes out of that total, but a small one
finishing beside a faster one still nets positive: 2 MB completing while
another gains 5 MB reads as +3 MB, and was reported as 3 MB/s against a
true 5 MB/s. The question is not whether the total fell but whether a
file left, so a reading now carries the set of in-progress names it was
taken across, and a rate is computed only when none of them has gone.
A download joining mid-window is still fine -- nothing left, so the
bytes that arrived are still bytes that arrived.

Stopping the sampler invalidated the timer but could not reach work
already queued on the sampling queue, nor the main-actor hop it ends
with. A reading in flight at that moment could land after the next
download had started its own session and seed that session's baseline
with bytes measured before it, making its first displayed rate a
fiction. A session counter now moves on every start and stop, is
captured when the work is scheduled, and is checked before the result
is recorded.

The decision is a pure function on a value type rather than a branch
buried in a main-actor method, so it is tested directly: six cases
covering a steady rate, a completion beside a faster download, a file
disappearing, a new download joining, a truncation, and two readings at
the same instant.

The source picker was drawing real app icons for the sources we had no

fix: keep live activities off the frontmost app's menus

A live activity draws into the strip of menu bar beside the notch, which
is the same strip the app's own menus occupy, so a running timer could sit
on top of them -- the Help menu especially, being the one nearest the
notch. Nothing about it was recoverable either: the only way out was to
turn live activities off in settings and back on again.

macOS offers no way to reserve that space. Menus lay out inside
NSScreen.auxiliaryTopLeftArea, and both auxiliary areas are read-only and
derived from the display hardware -- there is no setter, no entitlement,
and NSStatusItem reserves room on the other side of the notch. So rather
than asking for room, Atoll measures what is already there: the
accessibility API reports each menu's own position and size, which gives
the exact edge to clear, and the activity slides right by the overlap.

The shift is capped at the room remaining on the right, since a shift that
pushed the activity off the far edge would only trade one covered thing
for another. It returns to centre as soon as the frontmost app's menus
allow, so the notch is only ever off-centre while something would
otherwise be hidden.

The measurement runs off the main actor with a messaging timeout, because
it is a cross-process call and an app that has stopped answering must not
take the notch's UI down with it. It only runs while the notch is closed
and something is on screen, and a missing accessibility permission simply
means no constraint rather than a broken HUD.

Closes #793.

feat: keep the Mac awake from the notch

Adds a caffeinate control: a cup button in the notch header opens a
duration picker, and an IOKit power assertion holds the Mac awake until
the duration runs out or the user turns it off.

The assertion is held by Atoll's own process, so it is released if the
app exits for any reason -- there is no way to leave a Mac permanently
caffeinated by crashing. Turning the feature off in Settings also ends a
session that is already running, so the Mac can never be held awake with
no visible control left to stop it.

Settings › General gains the feature toggle, the notch icon toggle, a
default duration, and a switch for whether the display is held awake too
(off means the screen may still sleep while the system stays up). A
global shortcut toggles the default duration from anywhere.

The countdown and expiry logic are pulled out as pure statics and
covered by tests; the assertion itself is IOKit state and is not.

feat: per-app volume and mute from the notch

Gives each app its own volume and mute, independent of the system
volume. A sliders button in the notch header lists whatever CoreAudio
has an audio process for, playing apps first.

macOS only allows this one way: a process tap with `mutedWhenTapped`
silences the app's own path to the device, and a private stacked
aggregate device -- the tap plus the real output device -- gives us an
IO callback that scales the samples and writes them back out. That is
also why a tap is only created for an app whose level actually differs
from the default: Atoll must not insert itself into the audio path of
every app on the Mac just to list it. Apps at 100% and unmuted keep
their normal, untouched path to the speakers.

Each buffer ramps from the previously applied gain to the current one
rather than stepping, so dragging the slider does not click.

Taps are torn down when the feature is switched off, when the app stops
playing, and when the default output device changes -- an aggregate is
built around one specific device, and an abandoned tap would leave the
app muted with nothing rendering it.

The four CoreAudio process lookups the visualizer tap already had are
now shared as `AudioProcessQuery` rather than duplicated.

The tap is refused without audio recording permission, which the popover
now says out loud instead of leaving a dead slider on screen.

Off by default. Settings › Devices has the toggle, the notch icon, and a
reset. The pure decisions -- which apps get a tap, at what gain, how
helper processes fold into the parent app, row order -- are covered by
tests; CoreAudio itself is not.

feat: pin lyrics under the closed notch

The lyrics panel only exists while the notch is open, so following along
means holding the pointer over the notch. A pin on the panel header
keeps the line currently being sung under the notch after it closes.

Only the current line is shown, on one line: there is no room under a
closed notch for a list, and a wrapping lyric would grow the strip from
frame to frame as the words changed. It uses the same word-by-word sweep
as the panel, frozen while paused so a paused notch is not animating.

Hidden while a sneak peek is up -- both draw in the same strip below the
notch, and stacking them would shove the notch's own content around
every time the volume changed.

Also toggleable from Settings › Media, and the bounds check that decides
whether there is a line to draw is covered by tests: -1 before the first
line and an index outliving a shorter set of lyrics are both real states
that would otherwise trap on a subscript.

fix: keep the pinned lyric a caption, not a full-width slab

The strip claimed `maxWidth: .infinity`, and the closed notch sizes
itself to its content -- so a pinned lyric stretched the whole panel
across the screen.

It is now capped, and drawn as a plain single-line Text swept as one
rather than with the panel's word-by-word layout: that layout exists to
sweep a wrapped line in reading order, and this is deliberately one
line, where a line too long for the cap truncates instead of wrapping. A
second row would have grown the panel downwards from lyric to lyric.

fix: stop the pinned lyric reshaping the notch, and fade it in

Two problems with the strip, both from how it sat in the layout.

It demanded its own width, and the closed notch panel sizes to its
widest child -- so a long lyric stretched the panel, and the music row,

now fills offered width through a GeometryReader, the way the music

fix: show untimed lyrics as lines instead of one enormous line

When a track has only plain lyrics, the entire body was kept as a single
LyricLine at timestamp 0. Everything downstream then treated the whole
song as the line currently being sung: the highlight swept across all of
it at once, cutting through the middle of whichever word it reached.

Plain bodies are now split into the lines they are written as, and
carried as untimed. Untimed lyrics leave the current index at -1 rather
than letting the search settle on the last line -- they all share
timestamp 0, so it otherwise picked the end of the song and stayed there
-- and the sync loop does not start at all, since there is nothing for it
to follow.

The words are still there to read. Nothing claims to know where in them
you are, because nothing does.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix: choose lyrics that have timings over lyrics that merely match better

Carrying timings was worth three points in the match ranking, against
twenty available from the title, artist and album. A result with no
timings but an exactly matching album therefore beat one that had them
and agreed a little less precisely, and the song displayed as plain text
with no line ever lit -- even though timed lyrics for it existed.

Whether the words can be followed at all is a larger difference than
which pressing they came from, so it is decided before the score is
consulted, and the score now only separates results that are alike in it.

fix(llm-usage): parse Claude quota reset times with fractional seconds

The usage endpoint returns resets_at like 2026-07-03T00:30:00.282668+00:00.
The default ISO8601DateFormatter rejects fractional seconds, so the parsed
date was nil and the card never showed its 'resets in' countdown. Try the
fractional form first and fall back to the plain one.

Fixes #810

fix(llm-usage): keep the usage tab at the normal tab height

#552 made the provider cards equal in height by hard-coding 188 pt per card
and raising the tab's minimum height to 220 pt, 20 pt above every other
tab. The fixed card height also left blank space under shorter cards, and
the extra vertical room let the Antigravity title wrap next to its pool
picker.

Keep the intent (equal, centred cards) but let each card stretch to the
height the panel already offers instead of reserving a fixed size, drop
the 220 pt clamp, and keep the card title on one line.

feat(llm-usage): price current models, cache tokens and Codex by model

#683 taught getPricing to normalise Claude ids but left pricing.json to the
update-pricing workflow, which tracked four retired ids (three of them no
longer on OpenRouter, so their rows stayed empty). Every current model
therefore resolved to 'est. n/a'. Codex never priced at all: token_count
records carry no model name and were tagged with the placeholder 'codex'.

- Regenerate pricing.json from OpenRouter for the Claude 4.x/5, GPT-5.x /
  codex and Gemini 3.x families (72 models) and make the workflow select
  those families by prefix instead of a fixed list; drop the empty rows.
- Merge the remote table into the bundled one instead of replacing it, so
  a lagging remote copy cannot hide bundled prices.
- Extend the id candidates: openai/ and google/ prefixes, dashed minor
  versions converted to dotted ones (claude-fable-5-1 -> claude-fable-5.1),
  the fable family, Antigravity tier suffixes stripped, and a -preview
  variant.
- Tag Codex usage records with the model named by the session's latest
  turn_context record.
- Carry cache_read / cache_write rates in the table, keep cache-read and
  cache-write prompt tokens apart from uncached ones for Claude and Codex,
  and price them at the cache rates (falling back to the prompt rate when a
  model has none), so cache hits are no longer billed at full price.

feat(llm-usage): Antigravity token usage, reset times and reliable server discovery

Language-server discovery (#638) parsed 'ps aux' only after waiting for
ps to exit. With a few hundred processes the listing exceeds the 64 KB
pipe buffer, ps blocks, and the 2 s timeout kills it with only the head of
the list read, so the desktop client's server was never found and the
provider silently fell back to the cloud/keychain path. Read the pipe
before waiting and list only pid + command line. Discovery also accepts
the desktop client's '--flag value' argument style and asks lsof for the
port when the server was started with '--https_server_port 0'.

With the server reachable, read every conversation touched in the last
week (GetAllCascadeTrajectories / GetCascadeTrajectorySteps) and price
the per-reply modelUsage counters like the Claude and Codex log parsers,
translating the server's placeholder model ids through GetUserStatus.
The card shows Today / Week token totals and cost in place of the pool
rows, which repeated the gauges above and printed the remaining fraction
as a dollar amount.

The reset time parsed from the quota response is now carried on
ModelUsage so the Session / Weekly gauges show their countdown again;
it was dropped when the gauges were rebuilt from pool data.

fix: write the refreshed Claude OAuth pair back to its source

When the Claude Code access token expired, Atoll used the shared refresh
token to get a new pair, kept it in memory and left the old pair in the
credentials file / Keychain. Refresh tokens are single-use, so the stored
copy was dead from that moment: the next Atoll launch could not refresh
it ("Quota unavailable"), and Claude Code could not either and dropped
to logged out.

Store the rotated pair where it was read from, keeping every field Claude
Code puts there. Refresh only once the token has actually expired rather
than five minutes early, and re-read the source first in case Claude Code
already rotated it. A logged-out credential (empty tokens, expiresAt 0)
is treated as no credential instead of something to refresh.

fix: scope the Keychain write-back to the item that was read

SecItemUpdate writes every item its query matches, and service alone can
match several generic passwords with different accounts. Carry the
account of the item freshestGenericPassword chose through
CredentialSource and put it in the update query.
